subject: Private deployment connectivity: VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs site-to-site VPN — BlueHarbor

Subject: Re: Quick ask — preferred connectivity for private deployment

Hi Mina,

Thanks again for the walkthrough yesterday. BlueHarbor is moving to a private deployment of Redwood and our security/network teams are debating three options: VPC peering, PrivateLink (interface endpoints), or a site-to-site (S2S) VPN to our on-prem colo. Our top priorities are:
- Strong isolation (no cross-account accidental access)
- Minimal latency jitter for real-time scoring (p50 target ~20ms)
- Clear egress/cost predictability for budgeting
- Simplicity in our ops runbook (we have limited staff)

Would love your recommendation (and any decision matrix) — also attaching our current rack diagram (see blueharbor_onprem_flowchart.png). Can we get a short write-up we can hand to our network team?

— Nathan

Nathan — thanks for the clear priorities and the diagram. High level first: there is no single "always best" choice; each pattern trades off security, operational complexity, and cost. I put together a concise recommendation and a short matrix (attached: redwood_vpc_privatelink_matrix.xlsx), but summary here:

- VPC peering: simplest routing, low latency inside cloud, but cross-account peering implies broader network visibility and you may need NAT/route hygiene to avoid accidental access; works best when both sides are in the same cloud account family and you want minimal proxying.

- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): stronger surface-area isolation and doesn't require route propagation between VPCs; typically easiest to satisfy security teams because access is limited to specific ENIs/endpoints and traffic is scoped to the endpoint. Slightly higher egress cost per-GB and extra DNS setup, but easier to manage multi-account setups.

- S2S VPN: gives you direct control from on-prem to Redwood VPCs, good for regulatory isolation and predictable egress, but adds tunneling overhead, potential latency variability (depends on colo), and operational responsibility for failover.

Recommendation (short): For BlueHarbor — if you want the strongest isolation and multi-account friendliness with lower ops overhead, start with PrivateLink for production traffic and keep a low-bandwidth S2S VPN for administration/backup paths. Use peering only for internal-only, high-throughput test clusters (and only after strict routing policies).

I'll loop in Kimberly & Ben for a short technical pros/cons and concrete DN S/ACL checklist so you can hand to your netops team.

Next step: quick sync to walk through the matrix and the flowchart. Is Thursday 10am PT possible?

Best,
Mina Haddad

Team — forwarding BlueHarbor's ask and our initial recommendation. Key constraints: low p50 latency (~20ms target), strong isolation, limited ops headcount. Please add tech details we should include in the deliverable: routing implications, DNS patterns, NAT/hairpin concerns, monitoring and failover notes.

My starter notes (please edit):
- Routing: Peering requires routes in both VPC route tables and can inadvertently expose subnet ranges; need strict CIDR scoping and deny-rules on our side.
- DNS: PrivateLink requires endpoint-specific DNS names (we will provide CNAME records) and split-horizon DNS configuration on their side if they want plain hostnames.
- TLS & auth: All options should use mTLS at the application layer when possible; PrivateLink adds an extra network boundary but doesn't replace mTLS.
- Egress/costs: PrivateLink typically costs more per-GB; peering offloads to VPC egress pricing; S2S may add carrier/colo charges.
- Observability: Ensure TCP/TLS metrics, per-endpoint token-level logging, and traceroute traces are available.

Kimberly — can you add the specific security controls we should recommend (SG rules, recommended subnet layout)? Ben — can you add expected latency overheads (best/worst case) and an ops play for VPN failover? Sean — anything on multiregion routing or cross-account IAM constraints?

Thanks — Mina

+1 on Mina's recommendation. Adding concrete numbers and a short ops sanity-check:

- Latency:
  - VPC peering: typically adds ~1-3ms inside the same region for straight L3 routing. Excellent for p50/p95 in-cloud scoring.
  - PrivateLink: typically +2-5ms due to endpoint ENI hops and NLB pathing depending on cloud. Still fine for your 20ms p50 target but watch p95 if you have many short requests.
  - S2S VPN: highly variable; plan for +10-30ms depending on colo uplink and tunnel overhead — not ideal for sub-20ms p50 unless you have colocated WAN with very low RTT.

- Ops & Failover:
  - If you choose PrivateLink primary, maintain an S2S VPN as a warm failover for control-plane/maintenance (lower bandwidth). Automate health-checks (control-plane heartbeat) to fail traffic gracefully to a secondary region or endpoint.
  - For peering, maintain route automation and guardrails; one accidental route push can expose inter-VPC traffic. Limit IAM/service-roles that can modify route tables.

- Hairpin/nat: If BlueHarbor will call back into their own services hosted in the same VPC space, peering can cause hairpin scenarios — we should call this out and show NAT examples in the deliverable.

I can draft a short appendix with a recommended terraform snippet for each pattern and expected cost delta (rough numbers).

— Ben

Subject: Recommended design & next steps — BlueHarbor private deployment

Nathan / BlueHarbor team —

Thanks for the prompt. Attached is a short decision matrix (redwood_vpc_privatelink_matrix.xlsx) and the diagram you provided with overlay notes (blueharbor_onprem_flowchart.png). TL;DR recommendation and concrete next steps below.

Recommendation (production): Primary: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) into a dedicated Redwood VPC per environment (prod/stage). Rationale: tight surface area control, easier cross-account access in consumer-friendly way, and minimal route-scope blast radius.

Backup & operations: Maintain a low-bandwidth S2S IPsec tunnel from your colo to our control plane VPC for admin/metrics and as a warm failover. Rationale: gives you an out-of-band path for emergency access and audit collection without making it the primary data path.

Where to use peering: Reserve peering for internal test clusters that require highest throughput and are tightly controlled within your cloud account. Do not peering-prod to customer-managed accounts without strict route/ACL guardrails.

Concrete next steps:
1) Red team review and sign-off on PrivateLink CNAME/DNS changes (we will provide DNS template).
2) We will share the terraform snippets (Ben) and a short runbook for health-checks and automatic failover to VPN.
3) Schedule a 45-minute handoff with BlueHarbor netops to walk DNS, SG rules, and cost expectations. Proposed times: Thursday 10am PT (as suggested) or Friday 9am PT.

Notes & caveats:
- Costs: expect PrivateLink endpoint hour charges + per-GB data processing. We will include a line-item estimate.
- Monitoring: we will expose per-endpoint token-level logs and traceroutes; we recommend you enable packet capture on the colo side for the first 72 hours of traffic.
- Security: all traffic must still use application-layer mTLS and token auth; PrivateLink reduces network attack surface but is not a substitute for auth.

Attachments: redwood_vpc_privatelink_matrix.xlsx (decision matrix + cost delta), blueharbor_onprem_flowchart.png (annotated).

If that plan looks good I will circulate the terraform snippets and the DNS template and lock the kickoff time.

Best,
Mina Haddad
Principal Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference
